teeth. They sprouted anew. By the age of six and a half, I had unfortunately now gained a complete and fresh set. I had no interest in their welfare. By then, I had lost enough teeth to begin missing them in my day

day-to-day mastication of food, even if my tongue was now lavishing in the smoothness of its surrounds. I lost three more through medical intervention, and through necessity I gained my first set of dentures. With them came a revelation. It was only then, presented with the disembodied enamels, that the full

of this substantial link between food, tongue, throat and stomach became apparent. I began to place the form of the teeth above the function, vetting and analysing food for potential risk of the teeth falling foul. Many foods, in fact, became avoided. Avoided or mashed. Filtered, separated and mashed again.

prosthetic teeth pristine. My fascination with teeth soon began to spread outside the realm of my own and into those of other toothed animals. I marveled at their efficiency, their specificity. These wondrous beasts had no need to worry their minds about their teeth. They were blessed with immaculate design. I would take inspiration

Stairs to no end

Each one answered a leap. Not to ask questions is to live life asleep. I can't seem to forget that night when my father and I discovered the light.
As we entered the house, he put on a show. Family and friends, we were wrong all alone.
We must change our ways. We must make our life right. It will make us all strong if we believe in the light.
Then he called all us children, correcting our path. No more schooling, he said. No history, no math. There's no need for all that.

where you are. Your innocence will take us all very far. And to me, it made absolutely no sense. But my father explained, when you sacrifice, great light sees you as worthy of its price. But if you won't listen, won't do as you're told, the air that surrounds you will turn black and cold. Dark monsters will hunt you. And then, with a spark, forever, you will be lost in the dark.
Left alone, I decided. I had a task. I could not give up freedom. The freedom to ask.

Believers, shout your beliefs out loud. Surrender yourself to the will of the light. Have no doubts, no fears, no questions, no fight. Obey here and now and you won't be ignored. In the life that comes after, you will get your reward.

I then began climbing, the stairs to no end.

text_evidence.text: The tiny sparrow came to me by way of my parents' mailbox. They still collected the odd pieces of mail sent to me by those who didn't have my address.
USA 34

This particular postcard took me back to my post-college trip through India. I ended up stuck in Kopragown, a small village off the Godawri River in the Ahmednagar district. The monsoons washed away a section of the rickety railroad and left me marooned. It was there that I formed a routine of visiting the post office.
अह-पार

the only air-conditioned spot in the village. Mr. Chulkar, a willowy man with a mass of salt and pepper hair, worked there as the postal clerk. We drank chai and traded stories. Have you been to the Jackson Heights neighborhood in Queens? I shook my head. Srinivas, my identical twin brother, lives there. I tried to imagine this Mr. Chulkar taking the number 7 to 82nd Street.
He told me his brother fell sick when they were children, an aneurysm which led to a coma. Every night at the hospital, he would sprinkle water on his brother's toes, hoping it would jolt him awake.

He hated water on his feet. One night, the nurse walked in on me wearing a Bollywood mask. Popping out at Sinov's from the end of the bed, she screamed so loudly, it woke everyone on the floor, except my brother. They banned him for a day after he blew a conch shell in his brother's ear.

My family could not afford the medicine and our tiny hospital was not prepared for his long-term care. Rich Indians from the States adopted him and took him away. I have not spoken to him since he finally woke up from the coma. I think of him all the time, even 54 years later.
And then he told me, something that has stuck with me even 10 years later.
I have been taking my tea without sugar for a while now.

Today we will focus on our subject X, Vincent. Of course, his name does not make a difference. A tremendously arbitrary person in relation to an infinite universe.
SUBJECT X (VINCENT)

Just as arbitrary as the day itself, I suppose. His job as a photocopy technician has left him with an ambiguous desire for something more. He tried to legally change his name to Crouton, but couldn't be bothered with the paperwork and fees.

Vincent forgot his own face. He slipped into anonymity within this series of infinite doppelgangers. The recursive reflection had a profound effect. He was overwhelmed and arrested by the infinitude, caught in a feedback loop, a beginning indistinguishable from its end. What were the chances of X becoming Vincent? temperature, a dull but irritating migraine, his curiosity or lack thereof. Everything and nothing alter his route in curious and particular ways. This is subject Y, another variable that will change the outcome of subject X's day. The boy mistook him for an alien.

Five steps. Seven steps. And other times their encounter would be impossible. Here, X hasn't even left his apartment. He waits to talk to the landlord about a mysterious blue splotch on the wall. He wrote love letters in his mind and never mailed them. He made up her life story.

What kind of conditioner she used? Are her socks matching? Is she smiling? Perhaps she is in tears. Her name? Beatrice? Jacqueline? Maggie? He ran out of questions and let her carry on.
